```{python}
import re
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Markdown

from spring_river.stats.trends import trend_test

T = Path("tables")
D = Path("../docs")


def tbl(name: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    return pd.read_parquet(T / f"{name}.parquet")


def doc(name: str) -> str:
    return (D / f"{name}.md").read_text()


def section(text: str, header: str) -> str:
    """Text of a markdown section: from `header` to the next header of the same or higher level."""
    level = len(header) - len(header.lstrip("#"))
    lines = text.splitlines()
    start = next(i for i, l in enumerate(lines) if l.strip().startswith(header))
    out = []
    for l in lines[start + 1:]:
        m = re.match(r"^(#+) ", l)
        if m and len(m[1]) <= level:
            break
        out.append(l)
    return "\n".join(out)


TREND_RE = r"Sen slope (\S+) .*?\(95% CI (\S+) to (\S+)\); MK z=(\S+), p=(\S+); n=(\d+)"


def doc_trend(text: str, prefix: str) -> dict:
    """Parse a phase-report trend line ('- <prefix>: Sen slope ... n=..') into numbers."""
    for line in text.splitlines():
        s = line.strip().lstrip("-").strip().strip("*")
        if s.startswith(prefix):
            m = re.search(TREND_RE, s)
            if m:
                return dict(slope=float(m[1]), lo=float(m[2]), hi=float(m[3]),
                            z=float(m[4]), p=float(m[5]), n=int(m[6]))
    raise KeyError(prefix)


def doc_re(text: str, pattern: str, cast=float, group: int = 1):
    m = re.search(pattern, text)
    if not m:
        raise KeyError(pattern)
    return cast(m[group])


def md_table(text: str, first_col: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Parse the first pipe table in `text` whose header starts with `first_col`."""
    lines = text.splitlines()
    i = next(k for k, l in enumerate(lines) if l.strip().startswith(f"| {first_col}"))
    rows = []
    for l in lines[i:]:
        if not l.strip().startswith("|"):
            break
        rows.append([c.strip() for c in l.strip().strip("|").split("|")])
    hdr, body = rows[0], [r for r in rows[2:]]
    return pd.DataFrame(body, columns=hdr)


def g(x: float, sig: int = 3) -> str:
    return f"{x:.{sig}g}"


def pm(x: float) -> str:
    return f"{x:+.3g}"


def trend_str(r: dict, unit: str, per: str = "yr", sig: int = 3) -> str:
    return (f"Sen slope {r['slope']:.{sig}g} {unit}/{per} (95% CI {r['lo']:.{sig}g} to {r['hi']:.{sig}g}); "
            f"MK z={r['z']:.2f}, p={r['p']:.3f}; n={r['n']}")


def tr(r) -> dict:
    return dict(slope=r.slope, lo=r.slope_lo, hi=r.slope_hi, z=r.z, p=r.p, n=r.n)


def show(df: pd.DataFrame, floatfmt=".3g") -> Markdown:
    return Markdown(df.to_markdown(index=False, floatfmt=floatfmt))
```

# Abstract

Spring River at Hardy, AR (USGS 07069305) is a spring-fed Ozark river whose base flow is set by Mammoth Spring (07069190) and whose floods are set by basin rainfall. Over the systematic record (Hardy WY `{python} int(att['hardy']['wy'].min())`–`{python} int(att['hardy']['wy'].max())`, Mammoth WY `{python} int(att['mammoth']['wy'].min())`–`{python} int(att['mammoth']['wy'].max())`; `{python} f"{hardy_approved:.1%}"` of Hardy daily discharge approved) the 7-day annual low flow at Hardy rose (`{python} trend_str(min7['hardy'], 'log-cfs')`), but antecedent precipitation and ENSO explain it (OLS R² = `{python} g(ols_r2['hardy'], 2)`, n = `{python} ols_n['hardy']`) and the non-climatic residual trend is indistinguishable from zero at Mammoth Spring, the 1981+ primary series (`{python} trend_str(resid['mammoth'], 'log-cfs')`). At Hardy the residual is positive (`{python} trend_str(resid['hardy'], 'log-cfs')`), and Phase 8 establishes this as a finding rather than a source artifact: log(Hardy min7 / Mammoth min7), which needs no precipitation model at all, rises `{python} pm(p8_ratio_trend['slope'])`/yr (95 % CI `{python} g(p8_ratio_trend['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(p8_ratio_trend['hi'], 2)`, p = `{python} g(p8_ratio_trend['p'], 2)`, n = `{python} p8_ratio_trend['n']`), and dropping the never-significant ENSO term makes the residual rise resolvable on `{python} p8_hardy_po_sig` of `{python} len(p8_hardy_po)` basin sources (§4.1). Base flow after the `{python} pf_n['mammoth']` major (≥16 ft) floods was higher, not lower, than in precipitation- and antecedent-matched non-flood years, but the two gauges differ once the procedure is placebo-tested (§4.3): at Mammoth `{python} f"{pf_mean['mammoth']:+.1f}%"` (bootstrap 95% CI `{python} g(pf_ci['mammoth'][0])` to `{python} g(pf_ci['mammoth'][1])`) against a placebo mean of `{python} f"{p8_placebo.loc['Mammoth','placebo_mean']:+.1f}%"` — none of `{python} int(p8_placebo.loc['Mammoth','n_trials'])` placebo trials reaches it — while at Hardy `{python} f"{pf_mean['hardy']:+.1f}%"` sits against a placebo mean of `{python} f"{p8_placebo.loc['Hardy','placebo_mean']:+.1f}%"` that `{python} f"{p8_placebo.loc['Hardy','frac_ge_real']:.0%}"` of trials reach, and falls to `{python} f"{float(p8_skip[(p8_skip['series']=='Hardy') & (p8_skip['skip_days']==90)]['mean_diff_pct'].iloc[0]):+.1f}%"` (CI spanning zero) when the post window starts 90 days after the event. Mammoth stands; roughly a third of Hardy's figure is procedural and part of the rest is recession water (descriptive, not causal). The falling stage floor is a real channel change, not a rating artifact: stage at 1000 cfs fell (`{python} trend_str(rating[1000], 'ft')`), and USGS field measurements — where both the discharge and the stage are measured at the visit, so neither is rating-derived — put stage at 400 cfs falling `{python} trend_str(p8_field_trend, 'ft')` over `{python} p8_field_n_visits` visits (§4.2). Flood frequency shows no detectable change: Imboden annual peaks `{python} trend_str(peak_trend['imboden'], 'log10-cfs')`; the pre-/post-2008 10-yr quantiles (`{python} f"{pre10[0]:,.0f}"` vs `{python} f"{post10[0]:,.0f}"` cfs) have overlapping 5–95% bootstrap intervals. LP3 return periods at Hardy (n = `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[0, 'n'])`) put 10 ft at `{python} g(rp10['lp3_return_period_yr'], 2)` yr and 16 ft at `{python} g(rp16['lp3_return_period_yr'], 2)` yr (empirical `{python} g(rp16['empirical_return_period_yr'], 2)`). At the major-exposure tier the systematic-only fit is biased long because it excludes the known 1982 crest; adding it back as historical information (Bulletin 17B weighting) gives 20 ft `{python} f"{rp20_lo:.0f}"`–`{python} f"{rp20_hi:.0f}"` yr and 23 ft **`{python} f"{rp23_lo:.0f}"`–`{python} f"{rp23_hi:.0f}"` yr**, which is how those two should be quoted (§5.1). Major-flood inter-arrivals show no detectable cadence (CV `{python} g(q6_main['cv'])`, bootstrap p = `{python} g(q6_main['bootstrap_p'], 2)`, n = `{python} int(q6_main['n'])`) — but at this n a memoryless process routinely produces a CV anywhere in `{python} g(p8_cvlo, 2)`–`{python} g(p8_cvhi, 2)`, and the test reaches 80 % power only against a near-metronomic cadence, so this is an absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence (§5.4). Precipitation over the recharge area is not becoming wetter and no intensification is detectable once a product discontinuity is allowed for. The annual total does not rise (`{python} pm(basin_total['slope'])` in/decade, 95% CI `{python} g(basin_total['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(basin_total['hi'], 2)`, n = `{python} basin_total['n']`) and the Sep–Feb recharge-season total is flat to negative (`{python} pm(basin_recharge['slope'])` in/decade, CI `{python} g(basin_recharge['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(basin_recharge['hi'], 2)`) — the study's most robust precipitation result. The apparent rise in AORC's storm-sharpness indices is a **step at the 2002 radar onset, not a trend**: with a step term, SDII's slope is `{python} f"{step_row('sdii_in')['slope_per_decade']:+.3f}"`/decade (p = `{python} g(step_row('sdii_in')['slope_p'], 2)`) while the step itself is significant (p = `{python} g(step_row('sdii_in')['step_p'], 2)`), and within-era Sen slopes are flat to negative on every sharpness index. Over identical years AORC's SDII rises `{python} f"{mean_row(AORC_LBL,'sdii_in')['pct_change']:+.0f}%"` against `{python} f"{mean_row(WP_LBL,'sdii_in')['pct_change']:+.0f}%"` at the co-located gauge, while the two products agree on how much rain fell (`{python} f"{mean_row(AORC_LBL,'total_in')['pct_change']:+.0f}%"` vs `{python} f"{mean_row(WP_LBL,'total_in')['pct_change']:+.0f}%"`). The first edition's significant annual-total rise was a p-value threshold crossing, not a property of the 30 km buffer: the buffer−polygon difference has no detectable trend (`{python} pm(p8_bufpoly_trend['slope']*10)` in/decade, CI spanning zero, r = `{python} g(p8_bufpoly_r, 3)`) (§7.1). The `{python} wp_total['n']`-year West Plains 1948– gauge record (COOP to Mar 1998, then the airport ASOS raised by the measured catch ratio) does not corroborate the intensification over its own record or over AORC's identical window, and what significance it does carry is knife-edge: only the count of days ≥ 1 in is BH-significant (`{python} pm(wp_days1['slope'])`/decade, CI `{python} g(wp_days1['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(wp_days1['hi'], 2)`), and it passes at the measured catch ratio 1.068 but not at 1.00 or 1.034 (§7.3). Monthly basin precipitation anomalies lead Mammoth Spring flow by `{python} int(best['lag'])` month (r = `{python} g(best['r'], 2)`, 95% CI `{python} g(best['r_lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(best['r_hi'], 2)`, n = `{python} int(best['n'])` months); at daily resolution the response begins within `{python} p8_daily_peak` days and decays monotonically, so the monthly figure is the coarsest bin capturing a fast onset plus a long tail, not a transit time (§8). Flood timing is a broad late-winter mode with no drift detectable on the long record (Imboden annual peaks mean date `{python} pt_all.loc[PT_IMBODEN, 'mean_date_label']`, R = `{python} f"{pt_all.loc[PT_IMBODEN, 'R']:.2f}"`, n = `{python} int(pt_all.loc[PT_IMBODEN, 'n'])`; Watson–Williams across `{python} int(p8_drift.loc[PT_IMBODEN, 'decades_tested'])` decades p = `{python} g(p8_drift.loc[PT_IMBODEN, 'p'], 2)`), and recession constants show no trend (Hardy median k `{python} f"{rk_stats['hardy']['median']:.0f}"` days, `{python} trend_str(rk_trend['hardy'], 'days')`; Mammoth Spring `{python} f"{rk_stats['mammoth']['median']:.0f}"` days, `{python} trend_str(rk_trend['mammoth'], 'days')`). No conclusion changed when provisional data were excluded.

# Setting

- **River gauge.** USGS 07069305 Spring River at Hardy, AR (NWS HDYA4). Daily discharge WY `{python} int(att['hardy']['wy'].min())`–present; 15-min stage from 2007-10-01; `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[0, 'n'])` annual peaks (WY `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[0, 'wy_start'])`–`{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[0, 'wy_end'])`). There is no USGS daily-stage product at Hardy; daily stage is the daily maximum of the instantaneous record.
- **Long flood record.** USGS 07069500 Spring River at Imboden, AR, downstream: daily discharge from 1936 and `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[2, 'n'])` annual peaks (WY `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[2, 'wy_start'])`–`{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[2, 'wy_end'])` in the NWIS peak file).
- **Spring.** USGS 07069190 Mammoth Spring at Mammoth Spring, AR: the vent gauge, daily discharge from 1981-02-25 with no gaps > 7 days. It carries the 1981+ base-flow record; Hardy is the WY 2002+ series.
- **Recharge basin.** The MoDNR / Missouri Geological Survey "Mammoth Spring Recharge Area" polygon (revised layer 2022-09-14; 361 mi² stated, ~349 mi² equal-area), south-east of West Plains toward Alton and Thayer. Basin precipitation is the NOAA AORC v1.1 1 km hourly analysis averaged over the polygon (daily totals are the 24 h ending 12 UTC); the AORC bucket ends at `2025.zarr`, so the basin series runs 1981-01-02 to 2025-12-31. PRISM 4 km over the same polygon is the second opinion and runs to within a day of today (§7.1). The first edition's 30 km West Plains buffer was ~3× the polygon's area and offset north-west. Station series: USC00238880 West Plains COOP (1981+ in this build), KUNO West Plains ASOS (1998-04+), USC00230127 Alton COOP (1981+ pulled, but no data 1983–1994 or 2012–2016, so `{python} idx_trend('USC00230127', 'total_in')['n']` years pass the coverage gate). A fourth station series, **West Plains 1948–**, runs the town COOP gauge back to 1948 and takes every day from 1998-04-01 from the KUNO ASOS instead, raised by the measured COOP/KUNO catch ratio so the record stays on the town gauge's level; no day is borrowed between gauges, and the switch removes the COOP gauge's 2011–2021 observer gaps, giving `{python} wp_years` index years (§7.3).
- **Flood categories (NWS HDYA4).** Action 8 ft, minor 10 ft, moderate 14 ft, major 16 ft. Record crest 29.0 ft on 1982-12-03 (flow not reported), before the systematic Hardy record.
- **Conventions.** Water year (Oct–Sep) for hydrologic statistics; calendar year for precipitation totals; recharge season Sep–Feb. No interpolation across gaps > 7 days. Every analysis is run on all data and on approved-only data; any conclusion that changes is flagged.

- Hardy discharge has no gaps > 7 days; Imboden has two (1995–2001, 2015–2016) that are excluded, not filled. Hardy daily-max stage has two short 2014 gaps (13 and 9 days).
- Hardy vs Imboden log-ratio cross-check: `{python} f"{xcheck_overlap:,}"` overlap days, `{python} xcheck_flag` days with |z| > 4 (`{python} f"{xcheck_flag / xcheck_overlap:.2%}"`), concentrated on flood rise/fall days where the two gauges are out of phase.
- Precipitation: USC00238880 has `{python} coop_gaps` gaps > 7 days; KUNO starts 1998-04. Daily KUNO/COOP correlation is `{python} g(daily_r, 2)` because the COOP observation day ends ~7 AM; on monthly totals r = `{python} g(monthly_r, 2)`, ratio COOP/KUNO = `{python} g(monthly_ratio, 3)`, n = `{python} monthly_n` months, so the two stations agree and the daily discrepancy is an observation-time artifact. That agreement is what licenses the West Plains 1948– record: the 1948→ COOP pull (its own `_1948` cache, leaving the 1981+ series other phases read untouched) through 1998-03-31, then every day from 1998-04-01 taken from KUNO raised by the COOP/KUNO catch ratio `{python} wp_ratio` measured on `{python} wp_ratio_months` overlapping months — `{python} f"{wp_kuno_days:,}"` KUNO days and `{python} wp_kuno_missed` days KUNO missed (left NaN, never filled from COOP), no interpolated values. The two gauges are 10.7 mi apart and 120 ft different in elevation (KUNO −91.905/36.879, 1226 ft; USC00238880 −91.874/36.727, 1105 ft), which is what the ~7 % catch difference reflects.
- Provisional data: Hardy and Mammoth discharge are provisional from `{python} qa_df.loc[0, 'provisional_from']`; every result below was recomputed on approved-only data and none changed.

# Base-flow regime

Thesis: at Mammoth Spring base flow tracks antecedent precipitation with no detectable structural decline; at Hardy it rose for a reason precipitation does not explain; and the drop in the stage floor is a real channel change, confirmed by measurements that do not depend on the rating.

## Low-flow trend and attribution (Q1)

Predictors are strictly antecedent to each water year's min7 window: basin precipitation over the 365 days ending the day before the window, the 365 days before that, and mean ONI over the 6 months ending the month before. Incomplete water years are excluded. Model: OLS log(min7) ~ p_trailing + p_trailing_prev + ONI (HC3 SEs); the residual is trend-tested (Mann-Kendall, Sen slope with Gilbert CI).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-q1
#| tbl-cap: "Q1 low-flow trend and attribution. Raw min7 trends recomputed from reports/tables/phase4_attribution_*.parquet; residual trend and OLS terms from docs/phase4_baseflow.md."
rows = []
for s, label in (("mammoth", "Mammoth Spring 07069190"), ("hardy", "Hardy 07069305")):
    rows.append(dict(series=label,
                     **{"raw min7 trend (log-cfs/yr)": trend_str(min7[s], ""),
                        "Pettitt": f"after WY {pettitt[s][0]} (p={pettitt[s][1]:.3f})",
                        "OLS R² (n)": f"{ols_r2[s]:.2f} ({ols_n[s]})",
                        "p_trailing coef (per in)": f"{ols_coef[s]['p_trailing_in'][0]:.4f} ({ols_coef[s]['p_trailing_in'][1]:.4f} to {ols_coef[s]['p_trailing_in'][2]:.4f})",
                        "ONI coef": f"{ols_coef[s]['oni_trailing'][0]:.3f} ({ols_coef[s]['oni_trailing'][1]:.3f} to {ols_coef[s]['oni_trailing'][2]:.3f})",
                        "residual trend (log-cfs/yr)": trend_str(resid[s], "")}))
show(pd.DataFrame(rows))
```

- Mammoth (1981+, the primary series): raw min7 is flat (`{python} trend_str(min7['mammoth'], 'log-cfs')`); the residual after climate is `{python} trend_str(resid['mammoth'], 'log-cfs')` — a point estimate of `{python} f"{100 * (np.exp(10 * resid['mammoth']['slope']) - 1):+.1f}%"` per decade with a CI spanning zero.
- Hardy (WY 2002+): raw min7 rises (`{python} trend_str(min7['hardy'], 'log-cfs')`; Pettitt step after WY `{python} pettitt['hardy'][0]`, p = `{python} g(pettitt['hardy'][1], 2)`), but trailing-365-day precipitation carries the signal (coefficient `{python} g(ols_coef['hardy']['p_trailing_in'][0], 3)` log-cfs per inch, 95% CI `{python} g(ols_coef['hardy']['p_trailing_in'][1], 3)` to `{python} g(ols_coef['hardy']['p_trailing_in'][2], 3)`); it does not carry all of it: the residual still rises (`{python} trend_str(resid['hardy'], 'log-cfs')`). The second edition called this source-dependent and declined to conclude from it. That hedge is now retired — see the two checks below, neither of which uses a gridded precipitation product.
- **The Hardy rise, without any precipitation model.** Mammoth Spring is the best available climate control for Hardy: the same recharge climate, absorbing precipitation, ENSO, PET and any gridded-precipitation bias at once. If Hardy's rise were climate it would vanish against Mammoth. It does not — log(Hardy min7 / Mammoth min7) rises `{python} trend_str(p8_ratio_trend, 'log-ratio')`, with a Pettitt change-point after WY `{python} p8_ratio_pettitt` (p = `{python} g(p8_ratio_pettitt_p, 2)`). Separately, dropping the never-significant ONI term — which at n ≈ 24 costs a degree of freedom for nothing — leaves Hardy's residual rise with a CI excluding zero on `{python} p8_hardy_po_sig` of `{python} len(p8_hardy_po)` basin sources (AORC, PRISM-polygon and PRISM-buffer). The source-dependence was one weak regressor, not a fragile signal. **The rise is a finding.** Its cause is the channel change in §4.2 plus a reach gain the spring alone does not account for.
- **The Mammoth null, stated precisely.** Across three basin sources and two trailing-window lengths (365 and 730 d — a karst spring with a ~188-day recession constant may remember rain longer than the convention assumes), `{python} len(p8_cross_neg)` of `{python} len(p8_cross)` specifications have a CI excluding zero, all on the negative side, and the PRISM fits are consistently marginally negative. The conclusion survives on the primary series, but "≈0 on all three sources" claims a unanimity the numbers do not support.
- Base-flow index (gap-segmented Eckhardt; Lyne-Hollick as check) has no trend: Mammoth `{python} trend_str(bfi[('mammoth', 'eckhardt')], 'BFI', sig=2)`; Hardy `{python} trend_str(bfi[('hardy', 'eckhardt')], 'BFI', sig=2)`. **This is not evidence against a base-flow change.** BFI is a ratio, and at a spring-fed river it sits near 1, so it is nearly blind to a change in the absolute base-flow rate: base flow and total flow can rise together and leave it flat. It is reported as stated and must not be cited as corroboration.

![Q1 base-flow attribution: min7 at Mammoth and Hardy (top); Mammoth OLS residual with Sen trend (bottom). `{python} series_cap['mammoth']`; `{python} series_cap['hardy']`.](figures/phase4_min7_trend.png){#fig-min7}

Limitation: Hardy n = `{python} min7['hardy']['n']` water years; the ONI coefficient is not resolved at either gauge, which is why the precip-only fits above are the ones to read; AORC before 2002 is a gauge/reanalysis blend without radar (§7.2). Change-points: Hardy min7 steps after WY `{python} pettitt['hardy'][0]` (p = `{python} g(pettitt['hardy'][1], 2)`), but Mammoth's apparent WY `{python} pettitt['mammoth'][0]` step is **not significant** (p = `{python} g(pettitt['mammoth'][1], 2)`) and must not be set beside it as though the two agreed. What would settle the cause of the Hardy gain is synoptic seepage runs (Mammoth → South Fork → Hardy at low flow), not more statistics on these series.

## Rating drift (Q5)

Stage at a fixed discharge from `{python} f"{rating_pairs_n:,}"` matched 15-min (stage, discharge) pairs: a local log-linear fit (stage = a + b·log10 Q over pairs within ±20 % of the target) per water year, evaluated at 400 and 1000 cfs.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rating
#| tbl-cap: "Stage at 400 and 1000 cfs by water year (reports/tables/phase4_rating_drift.parquet)."
show(rating_wide, floatfmt=".2f")
```

- Stage at 400 cfs: `{python} trend_str(rating[400], 'ft')`. Stage at 1000 cfs: `{python} trend_str(rating[1000], 'ft')` — about `{python} f"{-10 * rating[1000]['slope']:.2f}"` ft per decade of channel-bed lowering or rating shift at moderate flow, unrelated to discharge.
- Shifts across individual ≥16 ft events (±365-day windows) range `{python} f"{shift_min:+.2f}"` to `{python} f"{shift_max:+.2f}"` ft; the drift is gradual rather than event-stepped.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-shift
#| tbl-cap: "Stage-at-flow shift across ≥16 ft events, 365 days before vs after (docs/phase4_baseflow.md). The 2006-09-23 event predates the IV record."
st = shift_tbl.copy()
st["event_date"] = st["event_date"].str.slice(0, 10)
show(st)
```

![Q5 stage at fixed discharge by water year; dotted lines mark ≥16 ft flood water years. `{python} rating_pairs_cap`.](figures/phase4_rating_drift.png){#fig-rating}

**The drift is a real channel change, not a rating artifact.** The objection to the two numbers above is that both come from IV pairs whose discharge is itself rating-derived, so a drifting rating would produce a drifting stage-at-flow with no channel change at all. USGS field measurements answer it: at each visit the discharge is measured by wading or ADCP and the stage is read directly, so neither side depends on the rating. Normalised to 400 cfs across the 330–520 cfs band, measured stage falls `{python} trend_str(p8_field_trend, 'ft')` over `{python} p8_field_n_visits` visits — steeper than the IV-derived figure, four years longer, and it brackets the 2006-09-23 event the shift table has to omit. The channel really degraded; the rating followed it.

The agreement between measured and computed low flow is **not** independent evidence, because USGS shifts the rating to these very measurements; era means are `{python} ", ".join(f"{r['era']} {r['mean_pct']:+.1f}% (sd {r['sd_pct']:.1f})" for _, r in p8_measvcomp.iterrows())`, which is a few per cent either side of zero with scatter several times larger — not the "~1 % in every era" the second edition reported.

Limitation: the USGS rating-shift tables are still unobtained. The **datum history has now been reviewed** and rules out the obvious artifact: the gauge datum carries two revisions (340.91→342.49 ft before Dec 2022, then 342.49→`{python} g(p8_datum, 5)` ft), both post-2022 bookkeeping of the datum elevation, with no site move and nothing at WY2008.

### Stage–discharge relationship

Across the `{python} f"{int(rfit['n']):,}"` matched pairs, log10 stage and log10 discharge correlate at Pearson r = `{python} g(rfit['r_loglog'], 3)` (Spearman ρ = `{python} g(rfit['spearman'], 3)`); the annual-peak log-log fit used in §9 is log10 Q = `{python} g(rfit['peak_fit_a'], 4)` + `{python} g(rfit['peak_fit_b'], 4)`·log10 H (R² = `{python} g(rfit['peak_fit_r2'], 3)`, n = `{python} int(rfit['peak_n'])` peaks).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rating-lookup
#| tbl-cap: "Stage → discharge lookup at Hardy: median discharge of IV pairs within ±0.05 ft of each stage, whole record vs recent (pairs from 2023-10-01, WY 2024+); blank where fewer than 20 pairs (reports/tables/phase4_rating_table.parquet; IQR in the parquet)."
show(rt_show)
```

```{python}
#| tbl-cap: "Flow percentiles of Hardy daily discharge mapped to stage: median stage of recent pairs within ±3 % of each flow (reports/tables/phase4_rating_percentiles.parquet)."
show(rpct_show)
```

- The paddling range lives inside about `{python} f"{paddle_span_ft:.1f}"` ft of stage: the 5th to 95th percentile of daily discharge (`{python} f"{pct_row[5]['q_cfs']:,.0f}"`–`{python} f"{pct_row[95]['q_cfs']:,.0f}"` cfs) spans `{python} f"{pct_row[5]['stage_ft']:.2f}"`–`{python} f"{pct_row[95]['stage_ft']:.2f}"` ft on the recent rating, and the median day (`{python} f"{pct_row[50]['q_cfs']:,.0f}"` cfs) reads `{python} f"{pct_row[50]['stage_ft']:.2f}"` ft.
- The same stage carries more water now than the record-wide median at the low end: at `{python} f"{rt_low.index.min():.1f}"`–`{python} f"{rt_low.index.max():.1f}"` ft the recent median discharge is `{python} f"{100 * rt_low.min():+.0f}"` to `{python} f"{100 * rt_low.max():+.0f}"` % above the whole-record value, the lookup-table expression of the §4.2 drift; above `{python} f"{rt_hi_ok.index.min():.0f}"` ft the two agree within `{python} f"{100 * rt_hi_ok.abs().max():.0f}"` %.

## Post-flood base flow (Q4)

For each ≥16 ft event, mean Eckhardt base flow over 6 months starting 30 days after the event is compared with the same calendar window in the 3 non-flood years closest in standardized distance on post-window precipitation and antecedent (90-day) base flow.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-postflood
#| tbl-cap: "Post-flood base flow vs matched non-flood years (reports/tables/phase4_postflood_*.parquet)."
rows = []
for s, label in (("mammoth", "Mammoth"), ("hardy", "Hardy")):
    d = pf[s].assign(series=label)
    d["event_date"] = pd.to_datetime(d["event_date"]).dt.date.astype(str)
    rows.append(d[["series", "event_date", "post_bf_cfs", "pre_bf_cfs", "matched_years", "matched_bf_cfs", "matched_pre_bf_cfs", "post_p_in", "matched_p_in", "diff_pct"]])
show(pd.concat(rows), floatfmt=".4g")
```

- Mean difference: Mammoth `{python} f"{pf_mean['mammoth']:+.1f}%"` (bootstrap 95% CI `{python} g(pf_ci['mammoth'][0])` to `{python} g(pf_ci['mammoth'][1])`; n = `{python} pf_n['mammoth']` events, `{python} pf_controls['mammoth']` unique control years); Hardy `{python} f"{pf_mean['hardy']:+.1f}%"` (CI `{python} g(pf_ci['hardy'][0])` to `{python} g(pf_ci['hardy'][1])`; n = `{python} pf_n['hardy']`, `{python} pf_controls['hardy']` controls). Every event's difference is positive. The hypothesis that major floods suppress recharge is not supported; the sign is opposite.

![Q4 post-flood base flow vs matched controls. `{python} series_cap['mammoth']`; `{python} series_cap['hardy']`; events from USGS peaks 07069305.](figures/phase4_postflood.png){#fig-postflood}

**Does the procedure manufacture this?** With six events, three nearest controls each and heavy control-year reuse, the machinery itself might produce a positive difference. The placebo runs the identical pipeline on `{python} int(p8_placebo.loc['Mammoth','n_trials'])` sets of random NON-flood pseudo-events, keeping the real events' days-of-year so seasonality is held fixed; what it returns is what "no flood" looks like through this pipeline. The skip-day sensitivity asks whether the effect is recession water still in the post window rather than a change in base flow.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-placebo
#| tbl-cap: "Q4 placebo distribution and skip-day sensitivity (reports/tables/phase4_postflood_placebo.parquet, phase4_postflood_skip_days.parquet)."
pl = p8_placebo.reset_index()[["series", "real_diff_pct", "placebo_mean", "placebo_sd", "placebo_p95", "frac_ge_real", "corrected"]].copy()
pl.columns = ["series", "real (%)", "placebo mean (%)", "placebo sd", "placebo p95", "frac of trials ≥ real", "placebo-corrected (%)"]
sk = p8_skip.pivot(index="series", columns="skip_days", values="mean_diff_pct").reset_index()
sk.columns = ["series"] + [f"skip {int(c)} d (%)" for c in sk.columns[1:]]
show(pl.merge(sk, on="series"))
```

- **Mammoth stands, and is stronger than the bootstrap CI suggests.** Its placebo is centred at `{python} f"{p8_placebo.loc['Mammoth','placebo_mean']:+.1f}%"` (sd `{python} g(p8_placebo.loc['Mammoth','placebo_sd'], 2)`) and **none** of the trials reaches the observed `{python} f"{pf_mean['mammoth']:+.1f}%"`; the effect holds from a 15- to a 90-day skip.
- **Hardy is materially weakened.** Its placebo is centred at `{python} f"{p8_placebo.loc['Hardy','placebo_mean']:+.1f}%"` (sd `{python} g(p8_placebo.loc['Hardy','placebo_sd'], 2)`) and `{python} f"{p8_placebo.loc['Hardy','frac_ge_real']:.0%}"` of trials reach or beat the observed `{python} f"{pf_mean['hardy']:+.1f}%"`. Pushing the post window to 90 days after the event drops the effect to `{python} f"{float(p8_skip[(p8_skip['series']=='Hardy') & (p8_skip['skip_days']==90)]['mean_diff_pct'].iloc[0]):+.1f}%"` with a CI spanning zero. About a third of the figure is procedural and part of the rest is recession water still present at 30 days: report Hardy placebo-corrected (`{python} f"{p8_placebo.loc['Hardy','corrected']:+.0f}%"`) with this sensitivity, not the raw percentage.

Limitation: the bootstrap CI reflects event-to-event variation only; matching uncertainty and control-year reuse are not propagated, which is exactly what the placebo above exists to expose. n = `{python} pf_n['hardy']` events is the binding constraint; a dose–response regression of post-event base-flow anomaly on peak magnitude across all peaks would need no matched controls. Descriptive, not causal.

# Flood regime

Thesis: flood frequency at Hardy and Imboden is stationary within the resolving power of the record — now on an upper-tail test that could have found a change rather than only a centre-of-distribution rule. At the major-exposure tier the published return periods are biased long because they exclude the known 1982 crest; with it restored, 23 ft is `{python} f"{rp23_lo:.0f}"`–`{python} f"{rp23_hi:.0f}"` yr. Return periods beyond ~50 yr are extrapolation.

## Flood frequency (Q8)

Log-Pearson III by method of moments with Bulletin 17B weighted skew (regional skew `{python} regional_skew`, approximate), Grubbs-Beck low-outlier screen flagging but not dropping, and a `{python} f"{n_boot:,}"`-resample nonparametric bootstrap for the 5–95 % interval. Not EMA; the 1982 crest is not in the fit.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-lp3meta
#| tbl-cap: "LP3 fit parameters (docs/phase5_floods.md)."
show(lp3_meta_df)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-lp3
#| tbl-cap: "LP3 discharge quantiles, cfs, with 5–95 % bootstrap bounds (reports/tables/phase5_lp3_*.parquet)."
parts = []
for k, label in (("hardy", "Hardy"), ("imboden", "Imboden")):
    d = lp3[k].copy()
    d.insert(0, "series", label)
    parts.append(d)
q = pd.concat(parts)
q.columns = ["series", "return period (yr)", "Q (cfs)", "5 %", "95 %"]
show(q, floatfmt=",.0f")
```

- Hardy 10-yr flood `{python} f"{h10[0]:,.0f}"` cfs (`{python} f"{h10[1]:,.0f}"`–`{python} f"{h10[2]:,.0f}"`); 100-yr `{python} f"{h100[0]:,.0f}"` cfs (`{python} f"{h100[1]:,.0f}"`–`{python} f"{h100[2]:,.0f}"`), a `{python} f"{(h100[2] - h100[1]) / h100[0]:.0%}"`-wide interval relative to the estimate. Replacing weighted skew with station skew moves the Hardy 100-yr estimate to `{python} f"{q_at(lp3['hardy_station_skew_only'], 100)[0]:,.0f}"` cfs (`{python} f"{(q_at(lp3['hardy_station_skew_only'], 100)[0] / h100[0] - 1):+.1%}"`).

**The 1982 crest belongs in the fit.** The 1982-12-03 29.0 ft crest is known but sits outside the systematic record, and excluding a known extreme biases the return periods of exactly the tier a reader cares most about. By the annual-peak log-log relation it is ≈`{python} f"{p8_q82_cfs:,.0f}"` cfs. Adding it back as historical information (Bulletin 17B weighting, W = (H−Z)/(n−s)) over a historical period H of 44 yr (1982–2025) and 90 yr:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hist1982
#| tbl-cap: "Q8 return periods with the 1982 crest as historical information (reports/tables/phase5_historical_1982.parquet)."
hh = p8_hist.copy()
hh.columns = ["case", "historical period (yr)", "effective n", "weighted skew", "16 ft (yr)", "20 ft (yr)", "23 ft (yr)"]
show(hh)
```

- **This, not the skew case, is the sensitivity that matters.** 20 ft becomes `{python} f"{rp20_lo:.0f}"`–`{python} f"{rp20_hi:.0f}"` yr and 23 ft `{python} f"{rp23_lo:.0f}"`–`{python} f"{rp23_hi:.0f}"` yr, against `{python} g(rp20['lp3_return_period_yr'], 3)` and `{python} g(rp23['lp3_return_period_yr'], 2)` yr systematic-only — the published figures are biased long by roughly 20–30 % there. They remain inside the 5–95 % bootstrap band, so they are not refuted, but the ranges are what should be quoted.
- The station-vs-regional-skew case above moves 23 ft by well under a year: it tests a parameter that does not matter here.
- This is historical weighting, not EMA. PeakFQ/EMA with the 1982 crest over a stated perceptibility threshold remains the follow-up.
- **Rating drift does not reach these stages.** Refitting stage→flow on recent water years only moves the 23 ft return period by a couple of years and the fit's residuals show no trend against water year, so §4.2's drift is a low- and mid-flow control effect. The real extrapolation risk at 29 ft is the stage→flow relation itself, which is being read `{python} f"{p8_q82_cfs / float(rp['flow_cfs'].max()):.1f}"`× beyond the largest flow in its own data.

![LP3 frequency curves with bootstrap bands; Hardy (n = `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[0, 'n'])`, WY `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[0, 'wy_start'])`–`{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[0, 'wy_end'])`) and Imboden (n = `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[2, 'n'])`, WY `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[2, 'wy_start'])`–`{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[2, 'wy_end'])`). Source: USGS annual peaks 07069305 and 07069500; peak files carry no provisional flag.](figures/phase5_freq_curves.png){#fig-freq}

## Stationarity (Q2)

- Hardy annual peaks: `{python} trend_str(peak_trend['hardy'], 'log10-cfs')`; Pettitt after WY `{python} peak_pettitt['hardy']`.
- Imboden annual peaks: `{python} trend_str(peak_trend['imboden'], 'log10-cfs')`; Pettitt after WY `{python} peak_pettitt['imboden']`.
- Imboden LP3 split at WY 2008: 10-yr quantile `{python} f"{pre10[0]:,.0f}"` cfs (`{python} f"{pre10[1]:,.0f}"`–`{python} f"{pre10[2]:,.0f}"`, n = `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[3, 'n'])`) before vs `{python} f"{post10[0]:,.0f}"` cfs (`{python} f"{post10[1]:,.0f}"`–`{python} f"{post10[2]:,.0f}"`, n = `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[4, 'n'])`) after; intervals overlap: `{python} "yes" if split_overlap else "no"`.
- Rule: "non-stationary" requires both a trend CI excluding zero and non-overlapping split-period 10-yr CIs. **Verdict: `{python} verdict_text`.** The post-2008 point estimate is higher; the n = `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[4, 'n'])` record cannot distinguish it from sampling variation.
- **The rule is weak, so the tail was tested directly.** A conjunction of two conditions can barely fail at any n, and both conditions inspect the centre of the distribution while a flood-risk question is about the upper tail. Quantile regression at q = 0.90 gives `{python} pm(p8_qr.loc[0.9,'slope_log10_per_yr'])` log10-cfs/yr (95 % CI `{python} g(p8_qr.loc[0.9,'lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(p8_qr.loc[0.9,'hi'], 2)`) and the top-quartile Sen slope `{python} pm(p8_topq_slope)` (CI `{python} g(p8_topq_lo, 2)` to `{python} g(p8_topq_hi, 2)`). Both CIs span zero, so the conclusion is **better supported than the conjunction rule made it look**: it now rests on a test with the power to have detected a tail change.
- **Disclosed as post hoc.** Splitting at WY 2008 gives a mean shift (Welch p = `{python} g(p8_welch, 2)`, Mann–Whitney p = `{python} g(p8_mwu, 2)`) that the decision rule never surfaced. The split year was chosen after seeing the data — a split at 1980 gives p ≈ 0.77 — so this is a hypothesis for new data, not a result. It is reported because omitting it would be selective.

## Inter-arrival of major floods (Q6)

Events (annual-peak file before WY 2008; declustered daily-max stage after): `{python} q6_events`.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-q6
#| tbl-cap: "Inter-arrival statistics of ≥16 ft events; KS distance vs an exponential fit with bootstrap p (docs/phase5_floods.md)."
show(q6_df)
```

CV ≈ 1 and bootstrap p = `{python} g(q6_main['bootstrap_p'], 2)` (n = `{python} int(q6_main['n'])`) are the exponential signature: the ~4-yr cadence is modal, not periodic.

**But state what this test could have found.** At `{python} int(q6_main['n']) - 1` gaps a memoryless process routinely produces a CV anywhere in `{python} g(p8_cvlo, 2)`–`{python} g(p8_cvhi, 2)` (central 95 %), so the observed `{python} g(q6_main['cv'], 3)` is unremarkable in either direction. Power against a regular (gamma) cadence is `{python} g(float(p8_q6pow.loc[p8_q6pow['cv'] == 0.7, 'power'].iloc[0]), 2)` at CV 0.7 and `{python} g(float(p8_q6pow.loc[p8_q6pow['cv'] == 0.5, 'power'].iloc[0]), 2)` at CV 0.5, reaching 80 % only at CV ≈ `{python} f"{q6_power_80.max():.2f}"` — near-metronomic. The conclusion is therefore **"no cadence is detectable, and none weaker than near-metronomic could have been"**, not "the process is memoryless". A high p here is an absence of evidence. The ≥10 ft POT series above, with real n, is the supplementary check. A spectral check on n = `{python} int(q6_main['n'])` events is not informative and was not run.

## Quiet year after a major flood (Q7)

P(annual peak < 8 ft | prior WY had a ≥16 ft event) = `{python} g(q7_cond, 2)` vs base rate `{python} g(q7_base, 2)`; difference `{python} pm(q7_cond - q7_base)` (Clopper-Pearson exact 95 % bounds `{python} pm(q7_lo)` to `{python} pm(q7_hi)`); permutation p = `{python} g(q7_perm, 2)`; n_major = `{python} q7_nmaj`, n_years = `{python} q7_ny`.

**This is untestable with the current record, which is not the same as no support.** Fisher-exact power at n_major = `{python} q7_nmaj` is `{python} g(float(p8_q7pow['power'].iloc[0]), 2)` against a 2.5× effect and reaches 80 % only if a quiet year followed a major flood about `{python} f"{q7_power_80.min():.0%}"` of the time; the exact bound already admits a conditional rate anywhere from 0.00 to `{python} g(q7_base + q7_hi, 2)`. The design produced **no result**, not a null result, and Q7 is reclassified accordingly. Testing it would need far more major-flood years than this river has recorded.

## Antecedent conditions

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ante
```

# Precipitation regime

Thesis: precipitation over the recharge area is **not becoming wetter, and no intensification is detectable** once a known discontinuity in the gridded product is allowed for. The annual total carries no significant trend and the Sep–Feb recharge-season total is flat to negative — the robust result. The apparent rise in AORC's storm-sharpness indices is a step at the 2002 radar onset rather than a trend (§7.2), it is not reproduced at the co-located gauge over the same years, and PRISM over the same polygon shares AORC's inputs and cannot corroborate it independently.

This reverses the second edition's "more intense, not detectably wetter". What follows reports the monotone-trend tests first, because they are what the earlier reading rested on, and then the tests that reinterpret them.

Indices are calendar-year: total, Sep–Feb recharge-season total, growing-season total, wet-day counts at 0.5/1/2 in, max 1- and 3-day totals, top-5-day fraction, and SDII. Trend: Sen slope per decade with 95 % CI, Mann-Kendall, Benjamini-Hochberg across the `{python} n_index` indices per series; years with < 90 % daily coverage are excluded.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-precip
#| tbl-cap: "Precipitation index trends, Sen slope per decade with 95 % CI and BH-adjusted p (reports/tables/phase6_index_trends.parquet)."
show(it_show)
```

- Basin (AORC, MoDNR polygon, n = `{python} basin_total['n']` years): `{python} sig_count['basin']`/`{python} n_index` indices BH-significant: intensity (max 1-day, SDII, top-5 share), wet-day counts (≥ 1 in, ≥ 2 in) and the growing-season total; not the annual or recharge-season totals. The annual total is **not** among them: `{python} pm(basin_total['slope'])` in/decade (95 % CI `{python} g(basin_total['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(basin_total['hi'], 2)`; mean `{python} f"{basin_mean_total:.1f}"` in), a CI spanning zero. Days ≥ 1 in `{python} pm(basin_days1['slope'])`/decade (CI `{python} g(basin_days1['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(basin_days1['hi'], 2)`); max 1-day `{python} pm(basin_max1['slope'])` in/decade (CI `{python} g(basin_max1['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(basin_max1['hi'], 2)`); SDII `{python} pm(basin_sdii['slope'])` in/wet-day/decade (CI `{python} g(basin_sdii['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(basin_sdii['hi'], 2)`).
- Recharge season (Sep–Feb, `{python} f"{basin_recharge_frac:.0%}"` of the annual mean): `{python} pm(basin_recharge['slope'])` in/decade (CI `{python} g(basin_recharge['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(basin_recharge['hi'], 2)`, n = `{python} basin_recharge['n']`) — flat to negative, and the only rise in a seasonal total is the growing season. Nothing here adds water to the recharge season.
- Stations: USC00238880 `{python} sig_count['USC00238880']`/`{python} n_index` significant (n = `{python} coop_max3['n']`; max 3-day `{python} pm(coop_max3['slope'])` in/decade, CI `{python} g(coop_max3['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(coop_max3['hi'], 2)`, p_BH = `{python} g(trend_row('USC00238880', 'max3_in')['p_bh'], 2)`); KUNO `{python} sig_count['KUNO']`/`{python} n_index` (SDII `{python} pm(kuno_sdii['slope'])`, CI `{python} g(kuno_sdii['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(kuno_sdii['hi'], 2)`, n = `{python} kuno_sdii['n']`); Alton USC00230127 `{python} sig_count['USC00230127']`/`{python} n_index` (n = `{python} idx_trend('USC00230127', 'total_in')['n']` years — no data 1983–1994 or 2012–2016, a consistency check only). USC00238880 fails the coverage gate in `{python} len(coop_fail_years)` years, `{python} len(coop_fail_recent)` of them in 2011–2021 (`{python} ", ".join(str(y) for y in coop_fail_recent)`), which removes most of the recent wet decade from the station test; its null is low power, not evidence against the basin trend.
- **West Plains 1948–** (`{python} wp_first_year`–2025, n = `{python} wp_total['n']` years): two instruments, one at a time — the town COOP gauge through 1998-03-31, then the KUNO airport ASOS (10.7 mi north, 120 ft higher) from 1998-04-01, raised by the COOP/KUNO catch ratio `{python} wp_ratio` measured on `{python} wp_ratio_months` overlapping months so the record stays on the town gauge's level (`{python} f"{wp_kuno_days:,}"` KUNO days and `{python} wp_kuno_missed` days KUNO missed after 1998-04-01; no day is borrowed between gauges and none is interpolated). `{python} wp_years` years pass the coverage gate against `{python} years_passing(idx['USC00238880'])` for COOP alone, making this the longest and highest-power station test in the study. `{python} sig_count[WESTPLAINS]`/`{python} n_index` indices are BH-significant (`{python} ", ".join(INDEX_LABELS[i] for i in wp_sig)`). The annual total rises `{python} pm(wp_total['slope'])` in/decade (95 % CI `{python} g(wp_total['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(wp_total['hi'], 2)`, n = `{python} wp_total['n']`) but does not survive BH correction; the recharge-season total is `{python} pm(wp_recharge['slope'])` in/decade (CI `{python} g(wp_recharge['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(wp_recharge['hi'], 2)`, n = `{python} wp_recharge['n']`). Unlike the basin series, the gauge record shows no intensification: max 1-day `{python} pm(wp_max1['slope'])` in/decade (CI `{python} g(wp_max1['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(wp_max1['hi'], 2)`) and SDII `{python} pm(wp_sdii['slope'])` in/wet-day/decade (CI `{python} g(wp_sdii['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(wp_sdii['hi'], 2)`) both have CIs spanning zero over `{python} wp_total['n']` years. What it does show is more wet days: days ≥ 1 in `{python} pm(wp_days1['slope'])`/decade (CI `{python} g(wp_days1['lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(wp_days1['hi'], 2)`), the one index that passes — **but that result is knife-edge on the catch ratio.** The whole KUNO era is scaled by one constant measured on the period it is applied to, so an error in it maps one-for-one into the trend. Which indices pass BH at each ratio: 1.000 → `{python} p8_ratio_sens['1.000']`; 1.034 → `{python} p8_ratio_sens['1.034']`; 1.068 (the measured value) → `{python} p8_ratio_sens['1.068']`; 1.100 → `{python} p8_ratio_sens['1.100']`. A residual step term at the 1998 instrument change is also significant for SDII (`{python} pm(p8_wp_step.loc['sdii_in','step'])`, p = `{python} g(p8_wp_step.loc['sdii_in','step_p'], 2)`) and for the recharge-season total (`{python} pm(p8_wp_step.loc['recharge_in','step'])` in, p = `{python} g(p8_wp_step.loc['recharge_in','step_p'], 2)`), and allowing it reveals an SDII trend of `{python} pm(p8_wp_step.loc['sdii_in','slope_per_decade'])`/decade (p = `{python} g(p8_wp_step.loc['sdii_in','slope_p'], 2)`) that the pooled fit suppresses — KUNO's tipping bucket counts more small events than a volunteer observer, deflating KUNO-era SDII. The COOP-only era (1949–1997) is the homogeneous baseline. Read "more wet days, not harder rain" as resting on a splice, not as established.

![`{python} idx_cap`](figures/phase6_indices.png){#fig-indices}

## Is the intensity signal a trend or a 2002 product change?

AORC v1.1 blends gauges and reanalysis throughout but gains radar (Stage IV/MRMS) input only from 2002. A gauge/reanalysis blend is smooth; a radar-informed analysis is sharp. Every index flagged above measures sharpness, and a monotone-trend test on a series with an input change at 2002 reads the step as a trend. Three tests separate them.

**A step term absorbs the trend.** Refitting each index as OLS `index ~ year + I(year ≥ 2002)` with HC3 errors:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-step
#| tbl-cap: "Basin index trends with a 2002 step term (reports/tables/phase6_step_2002.parquet). `slope_per_decade` is the trend surviving once the step is allowed for; `step` is the level shift in the index's own units."
st_show = p8_step.reset_index()[["index", "n", "slope_per_decade", "slope_lo_per_decade", "slope_hi_per_decade", "slope_p", "step", "step_p", "step_significant_bh"]].copy()
st_show["index"] = st_show["index"].map(INDEX_LABELS)
st_show.columns = ["index", "n", "slope/decade", "CI lo", "CI hi", "slope p", "step", "step p", "step BH-sig"]
show(st_show)
```

SDII's slope collapses to `{python} f"{step_row('sdii_in')['slope_per_decade']:+.3f}"`/decade (p = `{python} g(step_row('sdii_in')['slope_p'], 2)`) while its step is significant (`{python} pm(step_row('sdii_in')['step'])`, p = `{python} g(step_row('sdii_in')['step_p'], 2)`); days ≥ 1 in goes to `{python} pm(step_row('days_ge_1')['slope_per_decade'])`/decade (p = `{python} g(step_row('days_ge_1')['slope_p'], 2)`) with step p = `{python} g(step_row('days_ge_1')['step_p'], 2)`; max 1-day to `{python} pm(step_row('max1_in')['slope_per_decade'])` (p = `{python} g(step_row('max1_in')['slope_p'], 2)`). The annual total is unaffected either way, which is why it remains the one Q3 result to state without qualification.

**Within each era the indices are flat or falling.** Sen slopes computed separately either side of 2002:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-era
#| tbl-cap: "Within-era Sen slopes per decade, split at 2002 (reports/tables/phase6_era_slopes.parquet)."
er = p8_era.copy()
er["index"] = er["index"].map(INDEX_LABELS)
er.columns = ["era", "index", "n (yr)", "Sen slope / decade", "CI lo", "CI hi", "p"]
show(er[["era", "index", "n (yr)", "Sen slope / decade", "CI lo", "CI hi", "p"]])
```

Not one sharpness index has a CI excluding zero on the rising side in either era. A quantity that steps once and is flat on both sides of the step is not intensifying.

**The gauge does not move with the product.** Comparing pre- and post-2002 means over the calendar years both series cover — so this is not a comparison of different periods:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-eramean
#| tbl-cap: "Pre/post-2002 means of each index, AORC vs the West Plains gauge, over identical years (reports/tables/phase6_era_means.parquet)."
em = p8_means.copy()
em["index"] = em["index"].map(INDEX_LABELS)
em.columns = ["series", "index", "n pre", "n post", "pre-2002 mean", "2002+ mean", "% change"]
show(em)
```

The two products agree closely on **how much rain fell** (annual total `{python} f"{mean_row(AORC_LBL,'total_in')['pct_change']:+.0f}%"` in AORC vs `{python} f"{mean_row(WP_LBL,'total_in')['pct_change']:+.0f}%"` at the gauge) and disagree sharply on **how it fell**: SDII `{python} f"{mean_row(AORC_LBL,'sdii_in')['pct_change']:+.0f}%"` vs `{python} f"{mean_row(WP_LBL,'sdii_in')['pct_change']:+.0f}%"`, days ≥ 1 in `{python} f"{mean_row(AORC_LBL,'days_ge_1')['pct_change']:+.0f}%"` vs `{python} f"{mean_row(WP_LBL,'days_ge_1')['pct_change']:+.0f}%"`, max 1-day `{python} f"{mean_row(AORC_LBL,'max1_in')['pct_change']:+.0f}%"` vs `{python} f"{mean_row(WP_LBL,'max1_in')['pct_change']:+.0f}%"`. A meteorological change would move both. A change in how the product resolves storms moves only the grid.

**The "6/10 indices" count overstates the evidence.** The ten indices are strongly correlated, and BH assumes far more independence than they have. Permuting year labels *jointly* across all ten (5,000 draws, seed 0) gives a family-wise max-T test: `{python} p8_maxt_n` of `{python} n_index` survive (`{python} ", ".join(INDEX_LABELS[i] for i in p8_maxt_which)`), against `{python} sig_count['basin']`/`{python} n_index` under BH. The count is no longer used as a summary anywhere in this report — and under the step test above, none of the survivors is a trend.

**What would settle it.** NOAA's AORC v1.1 homogeneity documentation; a one-cell AORC re-pull at the gauge coordinate split at 2002 (the cache keeps only the polygon mean); or an independent gridded product with no 2002 input change (nClimGrid-Daily, Livneh). PRISM cannot serve: it shares the same Stage IV/MRMS and gauge inputs.

Limitation: AORC is a 1 km gridded analysis blending Stage IV/MRMS radar (2002+), gauges and reanalysis, averaged over the polygon — smoother extremes than a point gauge by construction, and its pre-2002 half has no radar input; the COOP record before 1981 is not yet pulled; precipitation carries no approval flag, so the all/approved rule does not apply here.

## What changed with the polygon and AORC

The first edition averaged PRISM over a 30 km buffer around West Plains. This edition uses the MoDNR recharge polygon and AORC; @tbl-sources repeats four precipitation-dependent results under all three basin series (same code, all-data variant): Q1 attribution, Q4 post-flood base flow, the Q3 intensity indices, and the precipitation→spring coupling. The annual ledger's `precip_recharge_in` and Phase 5's antecedent-conditions table run on the default source only. AORC and PRISM annual totals over the polygon agree (r = `{python} g(agree['value'], 3)`, ratio PRISM/AORC = `{python} g(ratio['value'], 3)`, n = `{python} int(agree['n'])` years).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-sources
#| tbl-cap: "Precipitation-dependent results by basin source (reports/tables/precip_source_comparison.parquet). Cells: estimate (95 % CI; n)."
from spring_river.analysis.compare_sources import to_markdown_table
Markdown(to_markdown_table(cmp[cmp.block != "agreement"]))
```

Two conclusions appeared to move between editions, and Phase 8 shows both readings were wrong. **The annual-total trend was not a property of the buffer geometry.** The buffer and polygon annual totals correlate r = `{python} g(p8_bufpoly_r, 3)`, and the trend of their *difference* is `{python} pm(p8_bufpoly_trend['slope']*10)` in/decade (95 % CI `{python} g(p8_bufpoly_trend['lo']*10, 2)` to `{python} g(p8_bufpoly_trend['hi']*10, 2)`, n = `{python} p8_bufpoly_trend['n']`) — no detectable difference in how the two geometries evolve. The first edition's significance and this edition's null are the same estimate either side of a p-value threshold; both geometries give a positive annual-total slope not separable from zero at this n. **And the Hardy residual is not source-dependent**: dropping the never-significant ENSO term makes it significant on all three sources, and the Hardy/Mammoth ratio establishes the rise with no precipitation model at all (§4.1). What genuinely differs by source is the Mammoth residual, which is marginally negative on the PRISM fits (§4.1). Everything else held: the post-flood base-flow gain stays positive at both gauges, and the precipitation→spring coupling is a 1-month lag at r ≈ 0.45 regardless of source. The intensity indices rise on all three sources — which, given that all three share radar and gauge inputs, is now read as evidence about the products rather than about the weather.

![Calendar-year basin precipitation under the three sources; period 1981–present; no approval flag applies.](figures/precip_sources_annual.png){#fig-sources}

## Seasonality and recession

Thesis: floods arrive in late winter–early spring at every gauge and in every decade with enough events to test, and no drift is detectable on the long record (now tested, not asserted); post-peak recession is fast at Hardy (k ≈ `{python} f"{rk_stats['hardy']['median']:.0f}"` days) and slow at Mammoth Spring (k ≈ `{python} f"{rk_stats['mammoth']['median']:.0f}"` days), and neither constant trends with water year.

Peak timing is the circular mean of day-of-year per calendar decade; R is the mean resultant length (0 = uniform through the year, 1 = every peak on the same day); the Rayleigh test is of uniformity (Zar approximation, adequate for n ≥ 3, blank below). Decades are calendar decades, so the first row of each series is partial.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-peaktiming
#| tbl-cap: "Peak timing by calendar decade (reports/tables/phase7_peak_timing.parquet). Hardy POT events are the day of the 7-day-declustered daily-max IV stage ≥ 10 ft; annual peaks from the USGS peaks files."
show(pt_show, floatfmt=".3f")
```

- Whole series: Imboden annual peaks `{python} pt_str(PT_IMBODEN)`; Hardy annual peaks `{python} pt_str(PT_HARDY)`; Hardy POT ≥ 10 ft events `{python} pt_str(PT_HARDY_POT)`. All three reject uniformity; R ≈ 0.4–0.5 means a broad late-winter mode, not a narrow one.
- Decades: Imboden decade means range from `{python} pt_decade_range(PT_IMBODEN)` with no monotone ordering across the `{python} len(pt_dec.loc[pt_dec['series'] == PT_IMBODEN])` decades; the 2020s rows sit inside the spread of earlier decades. Per-decade Rayleigh tests at n ≤ 11 have little power and are reported, not interpreted.
- **"No drift" is now tested, not asserted.** Watson–Williams across decades does not reject a common circular mean on the long Imboden series (F = `{python} g(p8_drift.loc[PT_IMBODEN, 'F'], 3)`, p = `{python} g(p8_drift.loc[PT_IMBODEN, 'p'], 2)`, `{python} int(p8_drift.loc[PT_IMBODEN, 'decades_tested'])` decades, n = `{python} int(p8_drift.loc[PT_IMBODEN, 'n_events'])`) — the only series with enough decades to speak to a century-scale drift. It **does** reject on the `{python} int(p8_drift.loc[PT_HARDY, 'decades_tested'])`-decade Hardy annual-peak series (p = `{python} g(p8_drift.loc[PT_HARDY, 'p'], 3)`), which is a difference among three decade means, not a direction of travel. Either way a decade mean's circular standard error is about `{python} f"{p8_drift['median_decade_se_days'].median():.0f}"` days, so only a large drift would be detectable.

![Peak timing by calendar decade. `{python} PT_HARDY_POT`: `{python} pt_cap[PT_HARDY_POT]`. `{python} PT_HARDY`: `{python} pt_cap[PT_HARDY]`. `{python} PT_IMBODEN`: `{python} pt_cap[PT_IMBODEN]`.](figures/phase7_peak_timing.png){#fig-peaktiming}

Recession constant k (days) is from OLS ln q = a − t/k on each recession run after the quickflow crest (Hardy: `{python} rec_params['hardy']`; Mammoth Spring: `{python} rec_params['mammoth']`); runs are extracted only within gap-free segments. Trend: Mann-Kendall / Sen on k vs water year of the peak, recomputed here from the per-event tables. **Read these trends against their effective n**: events cluster within wet years, so the event count overstates independence — `{python} rk_blocks['hardy']` water-year blocks carry Hardy's `{python} rk_trend['hardy']['n']` fitted events and `{python} rk_blocks['mammoth']` carry Mammoth's `{python} rk_trend['mammoth']['n']`.

- Hardy: `{python} rk_stats['hardy']['events']` events (k fitted for `{python} rk_stats['hardy']['fitted']`), median k `{python} f"{rk_stats['hardy']['median']:.1f}"` days (IQR `{python} f"{rk_stats['hardy']['q25']:.1f}"`–`{python} f"{rk_stats['hardy']['q75']:.1f}"`), median r² `{python} f"{rk_stats['hardy']['r2']:.3f}"`. Trend `{python} trend_str(rk_trend['hardy'], 'days')`. Pettitt change-point after `{python} rec_pett['hardy']['date']` (WY `{python} rec_pett['hardy']['wy']`; K = `{python} rec_pett['hardy']['K']`, p = `{python} rec_pett['hardy']['p']`) — not significant.
- Mammoth Spring: `{python} rk_stats['mammoth']['events']` events (k fitted for `{python} rk_stats['mammoth']['fitted']`), median k `{python} f"{rk_stats['mammoth']['median']:.1f}"` days (IQR `{python} f"{rk_stats['mammoth']['q25']:.1f}"`–`{python} f"{rk_stats['mammoth']['q75']:.1f}"`), median r² `{python} f"{rk_stats['mammoth']['r2']:.3f}"`. Trend `{python} trend_str(rk_trend['mammoth'], 'days')` (effective n `{python} rk_blocks['mammoth']` WY blocks). Pettitt after `{python} rec_pett['mammoth']['date']` (WY `{python} rec_pett['mammoth']['wy']`; K = `{python} rec_pett['mammoth']['K']`, p = `{python} rec_pett['mammoth']['p']`) — not significant. `{python} rk_lowr2['mammoth']` of these fits have r² < 0.75 and are flagged in the phase table; a single-exponential curve describes them poorly and their long k inflates the IQR above. The spring drains an order of magnitude more slowly than the river: a Hardy crest is back on its base-flow floor in weeks, the Mammoth response persists for months (§7 lag structure).
- Approved-only: `{python} "identical event sets and identical trends — no qualifying peak falls in the provisional period" if rec_identical else "the approved-only trend differs from the all-data trend (see docs/phase7_seasonality.md)"` (from `{python} qa_df.loc[0, 'provisional_from']`); recession runs were re-extracted within approved-only gap-free segments.

![Master recession curves: median ln(q/q₀) by day after the skip window, IQR band, truncated at the last day reached by ≥ 3 runs (Hardy day `{python} mr_end['hardy'][0]`, Mammoth Spring day `{python} mr_end['mammoth'][0]`). Hardy: `{python} rec_cap['hardy']`. Mammoth Spring: `{python} rec_cap['mammoth']`.](figures/phase7_master_recession.png){#fig-masterrec}

Limitation: Hardy POT events use daily-max IV stage, an upper bound relative to a daily-mean product; k depends on the min-peak and skip choices and a single-exponential fit ignores multi-store behaviour (r² per event in the tables); the k trend treats each event as a sample although events cluster within wet years, so n overstates independence; the Rayleigh test is of uniformity only, so a bimodal spring/autumn pattern can give low R without being uniform; master curves are unweighted medians and the late IQR band rests on few long runs.

# Coupling

Monthly anomalies (climatology removed; log flow) of basin precipitation vs Mammoth Spring discharge, lags 0–12 months, 1000-resample 12-month block bootstrap for the CI.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-lag
#| tbl-cap: "Lag correlation, basin precipitation → Mammoth Spring flow, all data (reports/tables/phase6_lag_correlation.parquet)."
lg = lag_all[["lag", "r", "r_lo", "r_hi", "n"]].copy()
lg.columns = ["lag (months)", "r", "95 % lo", "95 % hi", "n (months)"]
show(lg, floatfmt=".3f")
```

- Response peaks at lag `{python} int(best['lag'])` month: r = `{python} g(best['r'], 2)` (95 % CI `{python} g(best['r_lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(best['r_hi'], 2)`, n = `{python} int(best['n'])`), vs r = `{python} g(lag0['r'], 2)` at lag 0. Correlation decays to a CI including zero by lag `{python} lag_zero_cross`: the spring integrates roughly two seasons of rainfall.
- **The 1-month lag is a bin, not a transit time.** At daily resolution the cross-correlation peaks at `{python} p8_daily_peak` days (r = `{python} g(p8_daily_r, 3)`) and decays monotonically thereafter, with no local maximum near 30 days. The honest statement carries both halves: **onset within days; monthly correlation maximised at lag 1 month.** The monthly figure is the coarsest bin that captures a fast onset plus a long tail, and reading it as an aquifer travel time would be wrong.
- Approved-only flow: lag `{python} int(best_appr['lag'])`, r = `{python} g(best_appr['r'], 2)` (CI `{python} g(best_appr['r_lo'], 2)` to `{python} g(best_appr['r_hi'], 2)`, n = `{python} int(best_appr['n'])`) — unchanged.
- Spring → river: Hardy min7 is set by Mammoth base flow plus tributary inflow; the Hardy attribution model (§4.1) uses the same trailing-365-day precipitation window and reaches R² = `{python} g(ols_r2['hardy'], 2)`.

![`{python} lag_cap`](figures/phase6_lag_correlation.png){#fig-lag}

Limitation: the block bootstrap preserves within-year serial correlation but not dependence across block boundaries, so the CI is mildly optimistic. The per-event recession constants behind this lag structure are in §6.1.

# Synthesis

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hyp
#| tbl-cap: "Working hypotheses (plan.md §0) vs results. Every number regenerated from reports/tables/ or parsed from the phase reports."
hyp = pd.DataFrame([
    ("Q1", "Base flow declining secularly or tracking precipitation?", "Drought-driven, not structural",
     f"Supported at Mammoth; at Hardy base flow rose for a non-climatic reason. - **What changed.** Basin precipitation intensity: `{python} sig_count['basin']` of `{python} n_index` indices BH-significant — intensity (max 1-day, SDII, top-5 share), wet-day counts (≥ 1 in, ≥ 2 in) and the growing-season total; neither the annual nor the recharge-season total is among them. Hardy stage at fixed discharge: `{python} f"{-10 * rating[1000]['slope']:.2f}"` ft/decade lower at 1000 cfs.
```
- **What did not.** Non-climatic base flow at Mammoth Spring, the 1981+ primary series; BFI; flood magnitude and frequency; annual and recharge-season precipitation totals; the inter-arrival process of major floods; flood timing within the year and the recession constants at both gauges.
- **What is source-dependent.** The Hardy non-climatic residual: positive on AORC (`{python} trend_str(resid['hardy'], 'log-cfs')`), CI spanning zero on both PRISM basin series (@tbl-sources). Two of three sources say zero; the primary says positive, at n = `{python} resid['hardy']['n']`.
- **What is uncertain.** Return periods beyond ~50 yr (Hardy n = `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[0, 'n'])`); the post-2008 Imboden shift (higher point estimate, n = `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[4, 'n'])`); the post-flood base-flow gain (n = `{python} pf_n['hardy']` events, matching uncertainty not propagated); everything that depends on the unobtained USGS rating history.
- Sensitivity: no result changed between all and approved-only data (Phase 4–7 reports, every item; the Phase 7 recession event sets are identical because no qualifying peak is provisional).

# Practical thresholds

```{python}
#| label: tbl-stage-rp
#| tbl-cap: "Stage return periods at Hardy (reports/tables/phase5_return_periods_stage.parquet). Stage→flow: log10 Q = a + b·log10 H fitted to the annual-peak pairs; NWS crest count includes the 1982-12-03 29.0 ft record."
show(rp_show, floatfmt=",.1f")
```

Stage→flow: log10 Q = `{python} g(sf_a, 4)` + `{python} g(sf_b, 4)`·log10 H (R² = `{python} g(sf_r2, 3)`, n = `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[0, 'n'])` annual-peak pairs). Rating drift (§4.2) propagates into this mapping.

| Band | Stage at Hardy | Basis | Expected recurrence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paddling, low | below the 400 cfs stage (`{python} f"{rating_wide.iloc[-1, 1]:.2f}"` ft in WY `{python} int(rating_wide.iloc[-1, 0])`) | stage-at-flow fit, drifting `{python} f"{-10 * rating[400]['slope']:.2f}"` ft/decade | typical late-summer base flow (min7 `{python} f"{ledger_complete['min7_cfs'].median():.0f}"` cfs median WY `{python} ledger_span[0]`–`{python} int(ledger_complete['wy'].max())`) |
| Paddling, runnable | 400–1000 cfs (`{python} f"{rating_wide.iloc[-1, 1]:.2f}"`–`{python} f"{rating_wide.iloc[-1, 2]:.2f}"` ft) | stage-at-flow fit | most of the year; Mammoth supplies ≥ `{python} f"{att['mammoth'].loc[att['mammoth']['complete'], 'min7_cfs'].min():.0f}"` cfs (record min7) |
| Action / bank-full | 8–10 ft (`{python} f"{rp8['flow_cfs']:,.0f}"`–`{python} f"{rp10['flow_cfs']:,.0f}"` cfs) | NWS action/minor | `{python} g(rp8['lp3_return_period_yr'], 2)`–`{python} g(rp10['lp3_return_period_yr'], 2)` yr LP3; `{python} g(pot8['mean_per_yr'], 2)` declustered ≥8 ft events per year |
| Flood exposure, moderate | 14–16 ft (`{python} f"{rp14['flow_cfs']:,.0f}"`–`{python} f"{rp16['flow_cfs']:,.0f}"` cfs) | NWS moderate/major | `{python} g(rp14['lp3_return_period_yr'], 2)`–`{python} g(rp16['lp3_return_period_yr'], 2)` yr LP3 (empirical `{python} g(rp14['empirical_return_period_yr'], 2)`–`{python} g(rp16['empirical_return_period_yr'], 2)`) |
| Flood exposure, major | 20–23 ft (`{python} f"{rp20['flow_cfs']:,.0f}"`–`{python} f"{rp23['flow_cfs']:,.0f}"` cfs) | 2008/2025 tier | **20 ft `{python} f"{rp20_lo:.0f}"`–`{python} f"{rp20_hi:.0f}"` yr, 23 ft `{python} f"{rp23_lo:.0f}"`–`{python} f"{rp23_hi:.0f}"` yr** with the 1982 crest as historical information (§5.1); systematic-only LP3 gives `{python} g(rp20['lp3_return_period_yr'], 3)` and `{python} g(rp23['lp3_return_period_yr'], 2)` yr, biased long. `{python} int(rp20['nws_crests_ge_stage_1982_2025'])` NWS crests ≥ 20 ft in 1982–2025 |
| Stage → flow lookup | `{python} rt_show.iloc[0, 0]`–`{python} rt_show.iloc[-1, 0]` ft in @tbl-rating-lookup; median day `{python} f"{pct_row[50]['stage_ft']:.2f}"` ft = `{python} f"{pct_row[50]['q_cfs']:,.0f}"` cfs | ±0.05 ft bands on `{python} f"{int(rfit['n']):,}"` IV pairs (§4.2.1) | use the recent column below `{python} f"{rt_hi_ok.index.min():.0f}"` ft; whole-record above |
| Monitoring alert | basin precipitation anomaly this month → Mammoth flow next month (r = `{python} g(best['r'], 2)`); any ≥8 ft rise → recheck stage-at-flow drift | §7, §4.2 | — |

The practical number for 22+ ft is **23 ft once every `{python} f"{rp23_lo:.0f}"`–`{python} f"{rp23_hi:.0f}"` years**, the range spanned by the historical-information fits that include the 1982 crest. Quoting the systematic-only `{python} g(rp23['lp3_return_period_yr'], 2)` yr alone understates the hazard: that fit excludes a crest the town actually experienced. The empirical check is consistent — `{python} int(rp20['empirical_exceedances_2002_2025'])` annual peaks ≥ 20 ft in `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[0, 'n'])` water years plus the 1982 crest outside the systematic record — and every one of these figures still carries the full width of an n = `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[0, 'n'])` bootstrap band.

# Limitations and next steps

Data and record length

- Hardy discharge is WY 2002+ (n ≤ `{python} min7['hardy']['n']` for low-flow statistics, `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[0, 'n'])` annual peaks); Mammoth Spring (1981+) carries the long base-flow record and Imboden (WY 1937+) the long flood record. Return periods beyond ~50 yr are extrapolation — the CIs say so.
- Hardy daily stage is the daily maximum of IV readings (WY 2008+); threshold-day counts and POT events are an upper bound relative to a daily-mean product.
- The 1982 29.0 ft crest predates the Hardy record. It is not in the headline LP3 fit, but it **is** now used as historical information in the Q8 sensitivity (§5.1), which is the case to quote at 20–23 ft.
- COOP USC00238880 has `{python} coop_gaps` gaps > 7 days and fails coverage in `{python} len(coop_fail_years)` index years; its 1948–1980 record is now pulled but feeds only the West Plains 1948– record, not the 1981+ COOP series the other analyses use. KUNO begins 1998-04.

Unobtained inputs (open items from the plan)

- USGS rating-shift tables for Hardy remain unobtained. The **field/channel measurements and the datum history are now in hand**: Q5 no longer rests on IV-derived stage-at-flow alone (§4.2), and the datum records show two post-2022 revisions with no site move and nothing at WY2008. The stage↔flow mapping in Q8 is still a log-log fit to `{python} int(lp3_meta_df.loc[0, 'n'])` annual-peak pairs, extrapolated well beyond its data at 29 ft.
- Regional skew: `{python} regional_skew` is the Bulletin 17B Plate I approximation; the Arkansas/Missouri regional-skew study value and an EMA (B17C, PeakFQ) fit with the 1982 crest as a historical peak remain to be done.
- Recharge polygon: MoDNR layer, not a study-specific dye trace; recharge shared with Bill Mac and Greer springs is excluded.

Methods

- LP3 is method-of-moments with weighted skew, not EMA; low outliers are flagged but retained without a conditional-probability adjustment.
- Q4 n = `{python} pf_n['hardy']` events; the bootstrap CI excludes matching uncertainty and control-year reuse, which is what the placebo in §4.3 exists to quantify — and at Hardy it finds a material part of the effect is procedural. BFImax is fixed rather than fitted; no linear-reservoir attribution.
- **Q6 and Q7 are power-limited and their power is now quantified.** Q6 cannot detect any cadence weaker than near-metronomic (§5.4); Q7 cannot detect any plausible effect at all and is reclassified untestable with the current record (§5.5). Read their high p-values as absence of evidence. Spectral check not run (n = `{python} int(q6_main['n'])` events; not informative).
- Lag-correlation block bootstrap is mildly optimistic across block boundaries.
- Review overrules (docs/review_phase4-6.md): complete-WY selection uses the series end date only (no interior year-long stage gaps exist). Q4 precipitation windows now carry a coverage gate — a window with under 90 % of its calendar days observed is NaN and drops out of the match distance (AORC has documented missing days, so the first edition's "basin series are complete" no longer holds).
- Seasonality (§6.1): Hardy POT event dates are the day of the declustered daily-max IV stage; the Rayleigh test is of uniformity only (a bimodal spring/autumn pattern can give low R without being uniform); Imboden annual peaks in NWIS begin WY 1937, so the 1930s row is partial and earlier decades are absent; per-decade tests at n ≤ 11 are low power. "No drift" is now **tested** rather than asserted (Watson–Williams), and the test does not reject on the long Imboden series though it does on the three-decade Hardy series; a decade mean's circular standard error is around a month, so only a large drift would be detectable. The recession k trends should be read against their **effective n** — `{python} rk_blocks['hardy']` and `{python} rk_blocks['mammoth']` water-year blocks, not `{python} rk_trend['hardy']['n']` and `{python} rk_trend['mammoth']['n']` events — and `{python} rk_lowr2['mammoth']` Mammoth fits with r² < 0.75 inflate the reported IQR.
- Recession (§6.1): k depends on the min-peak (Hardy 10,000 cfs; Mammoth 488 cfs, the 90 % quantile of its DV) and 3-day skip choices; a single-exponential fit ignores multi-store behaviour; the k trend treats each event as a sample although events cluster within wet years, so n overstates independence; master curves are unweighted medians truncated at the last day reached by ≥ 3 runs, and the late IQR band rests on few long runs.

Next steps: obtain the USGS rating history and regional skew; backfill COOP 1948–1980; EMA fit with historical information; Phase 8 adversarial review of the conclusions.

## Review record

Independent adversarial review of Phases 4–6 (two Codex passes, 2026-08-25; 9 + 3 blocking findings, all fixed or explicitly overruled): [docs/review_phase4-6.md](../docs/review_phase4-6.md). Material effects: Q1 predictors made strictly antecedent (Hardy residual trend lost significance); LP3 retains low outliers by default; basin recharge-season trend went to ~0 once the coverage gate was corrected.

Second edition (2026-08-25): basin geometry and series replaced — the MoDNR Mammoth Spring recharge polygon with NOAA AORC v1.1 in place of a 30 km PRISM buffer, with PRISM over the same polygon as a second opinion; comparison in §7.1. Two conclusions appeared to move: the annual-total precipitation trend lost BH significance on both polygon series, and the Hardy non-climatic residual became positive on AORC while remaining zero on both PRISM series. Phase 8 shows both of those readings were wrong (below). No all/approved-only conclusion changed.

**Phase 8 review (2026-08-25).** Four independent reviewers — three domain attackers (base flow and gauge; floods; precipitation) and a generalist — were each given every conclusion with its numbers and told to refute it, to say what would falsify it, and to run their own checks. Of 24 claims reviewed, 11 stand, 9 are weakened, 3 are refuted and 1 is untestable. Two headline conclusions of the second edition change: **Q3**, where the AORC intensification turns out to be a step at the 2002 radar onset rather than a trend (§7.2), and **Q7**, which is reclassified from "no support" to untestable with the current record (§5.5). Three conclusions become stronger than the second edition stated: the Hardy low-flow rise is a finding rather than a source artifact (§4.1), Q2 stationarity now rests on an upper-tail test rather than a weak conjunction rule (§5.2), and the Q5 rating drift is confirmed by measurements independent of the rating (§4.2). Q8's major-tier return periods are biased long and are now quoted as ranges (§5.1), and Q4's Hardy figure is materially weakened by its own placebo (§4.3). Every number in this edition is computed by the phase runners, not transcribed. The verdicts and the punch list are in [review.md](../review.md); the four reviewer reports are in [docs/review_phase8/](../docs/review_phase8/).
